title: The Polarization-Index: A Simple Calculation to Distinguish Polarized From Non-polarized Training Intensity Distributions
authors: Treff G, Winkert K, Sareban M, Steinacker JM, Sperlich B
population: No participants: 15 training intensity distributions from nine published studies, mostly of rowers, with some of cyclists and of recreational runners
findings: The polarization index (PI) is log10((Zone 1 / Zone 2) x Zone 3 x 100), with the zones as fractions of the training volume (time or distance) in a three-zone model; the authors call a distribution polarized when the PI is above 2.00 a.U. and non-polarized at 2.00 or below.
If Zone 2 is 0, Eq. 2 puts 0.01 in the denominator; if Zone 3 is 0 the PI is zero by definition, and if Zone 3 exceeds Zone 1 the PI is not valid and must not be calculated.
Worked values in the text: 80-8-12 gives 2.08, 60-14-26 gives 2.05, 60-19-21 gives 1.82 (Zone 1 above Zone 3 above Zone 2, but too much Zone 2) and 74-11-15 gives 2.00.

Table 1 applies the index to 15 distributions: five exceed 2.00 (2.27 to 3.29), and the PI calls three distributions that their authors called polarized non-polarized (1.42, 0.91 and 2.00), two of them with 17 to 18% in Zone 2.

Limits the authors state: values from 0 to 2.00 must not be read as more or less polarized; the PI does not separate subtypes of non-polarized distributions; it is useful with Zone 1 at about 70 to 90%; it is not a surrogate for training load, because one value can come from different distributions and volumes; and, like any index, it loses detail.
limitations: A hypothesis paper: it collects no data and tests neither the cut-off nor the index against performance, adaptation or injury, and the authors call the cut-off an objective but not physiological definition. The examples are 15 distributions from nine studies, mostly of rowers and one of recreational runners. Eq. 2 is printed ambiguously; the Table 1 values (80-0-20 gives 3.18, 72-0-28 gives 3.29) fit log10((Zone 1 / 0.01) x (Zone 3 - 0.01) x 100), which a published commentary writes out, and not a floor on Zone 2 alone (3.20 and 3.30). The text's example that 90-5-5 and 74-13-13 both give 2.00 is wrong by its own Eq. 1 (1.95 and 1.87, recomputed on 2026-10-31), as the commentary also notes. The group that proposed the index in 2017 wrote the paper; the authors declare no conflict of interest.
implications: Use the index only to describe the zone mix of a plan or a runner: print it as a value beside the order of the zones (Zone 1 above Zone 3 above Zone 2 is the paper's polarized structure), never as a label, a target or a grade input.
Compute it on fractions of one volume measure so that percent, minutes and fractions give one value, and do not read values from 0 to 2.00 as degrees of polarization.
No engine rule uses it, and a hypothesis paper cannot support or change a Param.
